q: The skipper wants a loop in the end of a line that a swimmer can slip over their head and under their arms. It must not tighten. Which knot?
a: Bowline
o: Clove hitch
Rolling hitch
Reef knot
why: A bowline makes a fixed loop that does not slip or tighten under load.

q: The mainsheet runs through several blocks to the cockpit. What do you tie in its tail so it can never run out through them?
a: Figure-of-eight
o: Bowline
Clove hitch
Sheet bend
why: A figure-of-eight is the stopper knot: too fat to pass through a block.

q: The lazy-bag zip has broken, so you tie the furled main to the boom with sail ties. Which knot?
a: Reef knot
o: Sheet bend
Rolling hitch
Clove hitch
why: Tying round a bundle is the reef knot's job: it lies flat and unties easily.

q: You are on fender duty, and the skipper will want the fenders raised or lowered as you come in. What do you tie them on with?
a: Clove hitch
o: Bowline
Reef knot
Sheet bend
why: A clove hitch is quick to tie and easy to slide up or down to change the height.

q: The tender's painter is too short to reach the ring on the quay, and the only spare is a thinner line. Which knot joins them?
a: Sheet bend
o: Reef knot
Clove hitch
Figure-of-eight
why: A sheet bend joins two lines and holds even when they are different thicknesses.

q: The snubber must grip the chain when it is pulled along it. Which knot do you tie?
a: Rolling hitch
o: Clove hitch
Reef knot
Bowline
why: A rolling hitch grips a rope, spar or chain against a pull along its length.

fig.title: At anchor on all chain
lines: Snubber line ready on the foredeck
Skipper: "Tie it on to the chain"

q: You tied this fender on with a clove hitch. How do you stop it slipping?
a: Add a half hitch round the standing part
o: Wet the line so it grips the rail
Re-tie it as a sheet bend
Tie a figure-of-eight at the fender end
why: A half hitch round the standing part locks a clove hitch that works loose.

fig.note: The fender slips lower each time the boat rolls

q: You leave the tender on this ring while you have dinner ashore. Which knot will not shake loose as the tender jerks all evening?
a: Round turn and two half hitches
o: Clove hitch
Reef knot
Sheet bend
why: The round turn takes the jerks and the two half hitches stay put.

fig.note: Wash from passing boats all evening

q: You are making the stern line fast on this cleat. What does the line do first?
a: A full turn round the base of the cleat
o: A figure-of-eight over the horns
A locking hitch over one horn
A bowline round one of the horns
why: The turn round the base takes the load; then figure-eights and one locking hitch.

q: A new crew member finishes a cleat hitch with three locking hitches piled on top. Why does the skipper ask for it to be re-tied?
a: It can jam and is slow to free in a hurry
o: Three hitches can slip off under load
It wears out the cleat's horns faster
It makes the line too short to reach
why: One locking hitch holds; more can jam just when you need to let the line go fast.

q: You have coiled a mooring line and want to hang it in the locker without it coming undone. How do you finish the coil?
a: Wrap the end round the coil, pass a loop through and over the top
o: Tie the two free ends together with a reef knot
Tuck the loose end in among the loops of the coil
Wind the coil tightly round your hand and elbow first
why: Turns round the coil and a loop over the top hold it neat, and it is quick to free.

q: You are about to throw the stern line to a marinero on the quay. What do you do with the boat's end of the line?
a: Make it fast on the stern cleat first
o: Hold it in your other hand as you throw
Leave it loose on deck so it can pay out
Tie it to the guardrail with a clove hitch
why: If the boat's end is not made fast, a good throw can send the whole line ashore or into the sea.

q: How do you hold the coiled line to throw it ashore?
a: Split the coil: throw one half, let the rest run from your hand
o: Throw the whole coil in one bundle, as hard as you can
Wrap the coil round your hand and throw it as one
Throw the loose end first, then the whole coil after it
why: Half the coil carries the line; the rest runs out freely from your open hand without tangling.

q: You cannot hold the boat by hand. What do you do?
a: Take a turn round a bollard and hold the tail
o: Wrap the line round your hand for grip
Brace your feet and pull harder
Loop it round your waist and lean back
why: A turn round a bollard takes the load; a line wrapped round you can drag you in.

fig.title: Med mooring, crosswind
lines: You are on the quay with a stern line
A gust pushes the boat sideways
The line goes bar-tight in your hands

q: Ashore, you tie a mooring line to a post with a round turn and two half hitches while the wind pulls the boat away. Why take the round turn first?
a: It holds the strain while you tie the hitches
o: It lets the knot slip off in a hurry
It makes the line shorter and neater
It locks the hitches so they never undo
why: The friction of the full turn holds the load, so the half hitches are tied in slack line.

q: You have just left the marina and the mooring lines lie in a heap in the cockpit. What do you do?
a: Coil and stow them so none can trail over the side
o: Leave them out, ready for tonight's berth
Hang them over the guardrail to dry
Throw them down below into the saloon
why: A loose line can slip over the side and wrap round the propeller, or trip someone.

q: You have these three jobs to do. Which knots do you tie, in order?
a: Sheet bend, clove hitch, bowline
o: Reef knot, clove hitch, bowline
Sheet bend, bowline, clove hitch
Reef knot, rolling hitch, bowline
why: A sheet bend joins unequal lines, a clove hitch hangs fenders, a bowline makes a fixed loop.

fig.title: Three jobs
lines: 1. Join two lines of different thickness
2. Hang a fender on the guardrail
3. A fixed loop to drop over a bollard

q: You are about to throw the stern line. Where do you aim?
a: A little to the left of the marinero, upwind
o: A little to the right of the marinero, downwind
Straight at the marinero's chest
High over the marinero's head
why: The wind carries the line sideways as it flies, so aim upwind of your target.

fig.title: Throwing a line ashore
lines: Strong wind blowing from your left
Marinero on the quay, 4 m away
Line coiled, boat's end made fast

q: The line on this cleat is heavily loaded. How do you let out a metre safely?
a: Take off the hitch and figure-eights, keep a turn, ease round
o: Throw off every turn at once and let the line run out
Wrap the tail round your hand for grip, then uncleat it
Untie it completely and tie a fresh bowline further along
why: A turn round the base keeps control while you surge the line out against the friction.

fig.note: Skipper: "Ease the bow line a metre"

q: You are on the stern line as the boat reverses in. What do you do now?
a: Warn the helm and haul the line in fast
o: Throw the rest of the coil after it
Leave it there and throw a second line
Ask the marinero to fish it out
why: A line in the water by the stern can wrap round the propeller: the helm must know, and it must come out fast.

fig.title: Stern-to, reversing in
lines: Your stern line fell short, into the sea
It is sinking close to the stern
